speakers.name: Salmaan Allibhai
speakers.title: Chief Actuary and head of data and analytics team

exchanges.question: How have the newly disclosed new business quotes and bind orders trended year over year and quarter over quarter, and how should the KPI be viewed relative to submission growth? Is Kinsale willing to give up some accident year loss ratio for higher near-term growth?
exchanges.answer: Kehoe: the granular disclosure was requested by investors; the more granular the data, the more volatile, so do not overthink a 90-day move; across 25 divisions the market is competitive with opportunities in some places and slower growth in others. No quantification of quote or bind trends beyond prepared remarks. On loss ratio: all product lines are managed to a low 20s ROE or greater, pricing is adjusted in both directions, Q1 ROE was 24%, and he does not expect meaningful deterioration.

exchanges.question: Was anything one-off behind the accident year loss ratio, which was up 40 basis points year over year and better than expected, and how should it move given mix shift to casualty? Why did E&S Homeowners decline 22%, and how is Kinsale thinking about the 2026 reinsurance renewal given a below-average hurricane forecast and lower reinsurance cost?
exchanges.responderTitle: Chief Actuary and head of data and analytics team
exchanges.answer: Allibhai: nothing out of the ordinary and no one-time adjustments; there is some seasonality and Q1 is typically a little higher than other quarters. Winston: the high-value homeowners market has increased competition, limits offered are lower so average premium is dropping, while the Personal Insurance division (also a homeowners book) is still showing good growth. Kehoe: retentions, limits and so on are reviewed every year and have been increased many times over 17 years; he can't commit to how the treaties will be placed; renewal date is 6/1.

exchanges.question: How has competitive behavior in casualty from MGAs or admitted carriers changed over six months, and where has it been more stable? How much of the submission slowdown is demand versus pullback from irrational pricing, and what is being done to expand broker relationships?
exchanges.answer: Winston: over the last four-five months there is aggressive competition from fronts, MGAs and new companies in long-tail lines, specifically construction; premises liability is still strong and auto offers meaningful opportunities. Kehoe: the market differs for larger versus smaller transactions, and focus on small to medium accounts is a safe harbor; ex commercial property submissions were up 9%, an attractive rate; larger-account stress depresses growth until those accounts transition off the books. Kehoe is open to supporting experienced broker teams that start new shops in a principally wholesale model.

exchanges.question: Is there any change in retention, or is the gap between gross premium and submissions mostly pricing and large commercial property mix? Is there evidence that technology is enabling larger competitors to compete in small business E&S or admitted?
exchanges.answer: Winston: new business and renewal hit ratios have been consistent quarter to quarter for a long time, no big change. Kehoe: no, he is not seeing that; Kinsale made technology a core competency 17 years ago and the expense ratio is a proxy for its lead; with no legacy software it can adopt new technology including AI models more quickly; competitors would have to speak for themselves.

exchanges.question: Has commercial property pricing reset at a lower level or is it still drifting down? Is the expense advantage already fully deployed or will it be used to push the top line? How is the equity portfolio performing?
exchanges.answer: Kehoe: no good news on property; easier comps will come in the second half of the year because a disproportionate share of commercial property volume falls in the first six months. On expense advantage he did not say it was fully used; he cited conservative reserving, a 17-year record of favorable GAAP reserve development, and that growth is subordinated to profitability; gross written premium down 0.5% reflects a shift toward smaller average premiums. Equities are performing well: about 2/3 actively managed and 1/3 passive (mainly the S&P 500); since late 2022 they have lagged the S&P but roughly matched the Vanguard VYM benchmark, with less tech weighting.

exchanges.question: The analyst cited commercial property premium of $65 million in Q1 versus $375 million last year: what portion is the large property category facing competition? Could the low 20s ROE target need to come down to the high teens as capital enters the space at lower return targets?
exchanges.answer: Kehoe: no specific breakout, but average premium in that division is somewhere between $30,000-$40,000 per policy, versus maybe north of $50,000 a year or two ago, indicating a trend to smaller accounts. Winston: commercial property is the standalone division for large shared and layered deals, with small property broken out separately. On ROE, Kehoe is confident in a low 20s return on equity, about 15 percentage points above the risk-free rate (10-year treasury slightly below 5%).

exchanges.question: How does Kinsale's submission growth rate compare with the overall market or the E&S segment it competes in?
exchanges.answer: Kehoe: no specific information on the overall market; brokers canvass the market for their clients and he assumes there is some commonality with competitors' stats, but Kinsale doesn't really know.

exchanges.question: How is construction opportunity volume, and has activity slowed or been delayed? How did general casualty growth (about 11-12%) compare with Q4, given low 20s growth last year? Will cash from operations (up 8%) track net written premium and what are the free cash guideposts?
exchanges.answer: Winston: no delay seen; Kinsale doesn't focus on large project-specific policies, though some wrap projects out west and in the northeast are being delayed. Kehoe: no sequential general casualty stats to provide, pointing to the by-division premium and three-year lookback in the 10-K. Petrucelli: trending cash flow with net written premium is a good way to look at it.

guidance.current: Easier comps in the second half of the year, as a disproportionate share of commercial property volume falls in the first six months
